title: Devanagari
hookLine: a line of letters on a wedding card: why learn to read what already works when it's chanted?
carry: among letters, krishna is the letter a
tomorrow: a line runs across the top of the letters. what's it holding up?

lines: A LINE OF LETTERS ON THE FRIDGE.
WHY LEARN THE LETTERS AT ALL?
cards: A wedding card on the fridge. A sticker on a laptop. A line of text under a photo in the family group chat.
Letters with a flat bar running along the top, each one hanging from it like laundry on a line. Some people read it at a glance. To others it's a row of beautiful shapes.
That script is Devanagari, and year five opens with it. So, one question for today: if a sacred line already works when it's chanted, why learn the letters at all?

teach.b: Here's one answer the tradition gives, from the Bhagavad Gita. In chapter ten, Krishna names the places he can be found: among mountains, among rivers, among seasons. And among letters, he says, I am a.
Not a temple, not a star. A letter. Some readers notice something about the script itself.

teach.h: A SHORT A INSIDE EVERY LETTER.
teach.b: In Devanagari, a consonant written alone is never silent: it carries a short a inside it. Ka, not k. Ga, not g.
Unless a small mark takes it away, a is there in the letter, the way the Gita says the divine is there in the world.
Then the word for a letter: akshara. It also means the imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The Gita uses it both ways.
In chapter eight, the akshara is the highest, the imperishable. In chapter ten, aksharas are letters. So learning to read isn't only homework before the real thing.

The letters can be a way in. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. Muslim tradition holds that the first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, were a command to read.
In Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth."

teach.h: READ: WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.
teach.b: And a few lines on: "Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not."

teach.h: THE LETTERS CAN BE A WAY IN.
teach.b: Two traditions, each putting something holy right beside learning your letters. And one honest difference. In the Qur'an's words, God is the one who teaches, and the pen is how.
In the Gita's words, Krishna is found in the letter itself.

how: Hindu children and adults learn Devanagari at home, at weekend classes and from teachers who chant verses with them; some begin a new subject or school year by writing their first letters before Saraswati or Ganesha.

games.q: your cousin wants to read Sanskrit, but says there's no point unless she can read a whole chapter of the Gita by summer. she's ready to quit before starting. what fits today's lesson?
o: start with one letter, a. the Gita treats even that as a way in.
wait until there's time to learn every letter at once, properly.
skip the letters and learn it only by ear; sound is what matters.
games.why: Krishna says among letters he is a, the sound inside every consonant. the tradition honors the chanted sound too, but here the letters themselves are a way in, starting with one.

practice: Let a soft, open sound ride out on each breath: a, the way it sits inside ka and ga, mouth relaxed, no effort. Breathe in quietly, sound it on the way out, and let it fade into silence before the next breath.
Krishna's letter, said for as long as the bell runs.

wordCard.voice: Devanagari: the script with the bar along the top, used for Sanskrit, and for Hindi and Marathi too. Its letters are aksharas. Year five's first word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a letter or syllable, and also the imperishable; the Gita uses it both ways (8.3, 10.33).

carryVoice: For the road: among letters, Krishna is the letter a, the sound inside them all. Year five, day one.
